title: Who can appeal a consent decree?

scenes.dialogue: Hi, I am Ravishankar from LawWorld. No appeal lies from a consent decree. But does that bar stop a stranger to the compromise, whose rights the decree affects?
On thirtieth October, a two-judge Supreme Court bench of Honourable Justice J B Pardiwala and Honourable Justice K Vinod Chandran ruled.
scenes.shown: On 30 October, a two-judge Supreme Court bench of Honourable Justice J.B. Pardiwala and Honourable Justice K. Vinod Chandran ruled.

scenes.dialogue: In nineteen seventy five, the owner sold the land to the respondents' predecessor. Years later, his heirs agreed to sell it to a housing society.
scenes.shown: In 1975, the owner sold the land to the respondents' predecessor. Years later, his heirs agreed to sell it to a housing society.

scenes.dialogue: The society sued for specific performance, and got a consent decree in twenty thirteen. In twenty twenty two, the land was conveyed to the appellant.
scenes.shown: The society sued for specific performance, and got a consent decree in 2013. In 2022, the land was conveyed to the appellant.

scenes.dialogue: Strangers to that suit, the respondents appealed in twenty twenty four. The High Court restrained the appellant, then condoned eleven years' delay and granted leave.
scenes.shown: Strangers to that suit, the respondents appealed in 2024. The High Court restrained the appellant, then condoned 11 years' delay and granted leave.

scenes.dialogue: The appellant argued that Section Ninety Six, sub section Three, bars any appeal from a consent decree, and that a stranger to the compromise cannot challenge it.
scenes.shown: The appellant argued that Section 96(3) bars any appeal from a consent decree, and that a stranger to the compromise cannot challenge it.

scenes.dialogue: The Court disagreed. That bar, and the estoppel under Order Twenty Three, bind only the parties to the compromise. A stranger is not deemed to have consented.
scenes.shown: The Court disagreed. That bar, and the estoppel under Order XXIII, bind only the parties to the compromise. A stranger is not deemed to have consented.

scenes.dialogue: But a stranger needs leave, and must show prima facie prejudice. A consent decree faces no stricter test. Here, leave was rightly granted, with no view on the merits.
A stranger's knowledge can't be assumed from the decree's date; with the delay explained, condoning it was no error. The injunction wasn't disturbed; the appeals failed.
